name: Boost.Polygon (Voronoi diagram builder)
baseline: CGAL (Delaunay triangulation of points / segment Delaunay graph; CGAL-4.3-beta1 in the benchmark)
workload: Average construction time of the Voronoi diagram (Boost.Polygon) versus the Delaunay triangulation (CGAL, S-Hull) of random points and of random non-intersecting segments, uniformly distributed on a 32-bit integer grid, from 100 to 1,000,000 inputs.
claimed_speedup: Random segments, average construction time in seconds, Boost.Polygon vs CGAL: 100 segments 0.002284 vs 0.002985; 10,000 segments 0.2377 vs 0.3374; 1,000,000 segments 25.0 vs 39.09 (about 1.56x faster at 1M, derived from page data). Random points: Boost.Polygon is slower than CGAL (1,000,000 points 3.47 s vs 0.9023 s; S-Hull 6.603814 s). A second page in the repo (doc/analysis.htm) says Boost.Polygon's arbitrary-angle Booleans are 'roughly as fast as GPC at small scales, while algorithmically faster at large scales' and that a 2010 divide-and-conquer change gave 10X over its own older algorithm at 200,000+ rectangles; it gives no GPC numbers.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.7.3 with Boost 1.54.0, CGAL-4.3-beta1, GMP 5.1.4, MPFR 3.1.2; optimization flags are not stated (benchmark/Jamfile.v2 sets none)
hardware: Intel i5-7600 2.8 GHz, 16 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 13.04 64-bit (as printed on the page)
stars_or_usage: 70 stars; part of the Boost libraries
tradeoffs: Builds a Voronoi diagram (points and segments) with output coordinates at '128 machine epsilon' precision per the page, whereas the compared CGAL and S-Hull routines build a Delaunay triangulation with no output coordinates. No external dependencies (CGAL needs Boost, GMP, MPFR). The benchmark uses 32-bit integer input coordinates.
caveats: Mixed result: only the segment input wins. For points CGAL's Delaunay triangulation is about 3.8x faster than Boost.Polygon at 1M points (derived from page data). Voronoi and Delaunay are different outputs (the page notes the Voronoi diagram carries more information). First-party benchmark by the library author with an old setup (GCC 4.7.3, CGAL 4.3-beta1, Ubuntu 13.04) and no stated optimization flags. A WebSearch snippet of the boost.org copy (1_54_0) summarised the result as complete dominance over the CGAL Delaunay graph, which the points table in the repo copy does not support. boost.org itself was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the numbers were read from the same file in the repo. The page's CPU model (i5-7600) looks inconsistent with a 2013 setup; reported as printed.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'fast computational geometry engineering blog benchmark faster than CGAL Delaunay triangulation' surfaced the boost.org 'Voronoi Benchmark' page (page blocked here); numbers read from doc/voronoi_benchmark.htm and doc/analysis.htm in the boostorg/polygon repo

name: Bonxai
workload: README benchmark of a sparse 3D voxel grid: create a new grid from scratch, update the value of already allocated cells, and iterate all cells (dataset size not described).
claimed_speedup: Create 1165 us vs 25522 us (about 21.9x, derived from page data); Update 851 us vs 3824 us (about 4.5x, derived from page data); IterateAllCells 124 us vs 698 us (about 5.6x, derived from page data). README also states Bonxai is 'much faster and, in some cases, even more memory-efficient than an Octree'.
tradeoffs: Hierarchical sparse voxel grid influenced by OpenVDB rather than a multi-resolution octree; sparse and unbounded with 32-bit indices (about 40,000 km at 1 cm voxels per the README); core is header-only.
caveats: README labels the numbers 'preliminary' and says to take them with a grain of salt because they depend on how the data is stored. No compiler, flags, CPU or benchmark-code location is given in that section. The README also says the project is under development and built mostly for fun and educational purposes. Baseline Octomap is a robotics-mapping incumbent, not one of Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS or R-tree baselines, so this is borderline for the category.
found_via: Blogs / talks slice: no search query; checked directly on github.com while looking at voxel-grid and octree alternatives; evidence is the repo README benchmark section

name: GeometryOps.jl
baseline: GEOS (through GeoPandas/Shapely in Python and the 'geos' package in R)
workload: kadyb/vector-benchmark: 500,000 synthetic planar points and derived geometries; tasks are buffer, distance between points, intersects, sampling points in a polygon, CRS transform, and GeoPackage load/write; median seconds per task.
claimed_speedup: Median seconds, GeometryOps.jl vs GEOS-backed packages: distance 0.11 vs 5.37 (R geos) and 0.90 (GeoPandas); intersects 0.04 vs 0.08 (R geos) and 0.12 (GeoPandas); sample 0.04 vs 0.90 (GeoPandas); transform 0.08 vs 0.23 (GeoPandas); load 0.36 vs 0.45 (GeoPandas). Not faster: buffer 5.75 vs 4.07 (GeoPandas) and 5.65 (R geos); write 1.38 vs 1.28 (GeoPandas). Derived ratios (derived from page data): distance about 8x vs GeoPandas and 49x vs R geos, intersects 2x vs R geos and 3x vs GeoPandas, sample about 22x vs GeoPandas.
compiler_and_flags: Interpreted/JIT packages (Julia, Python, R); no compiler flags and no package versions are stated in the repo README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X @ 3.7 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
tradeoffs: Pure Julia, GeoInterface.jl-based, mostly 2D/2.5D geometry; not callable from C++ without embedding Julia. README warns the package is under heavy development. Includes OGC predicates, clipping (intersection, union, difference), simplification and more.
caveats: GEOS is measured through wrappers (GeoPandas/Shapely, R 'geos'), so wrapper and marshalling overhead is part of the baseline times; the 5.37 s R geos distance time looks like such an artifact. Buffer and write are not faster. Numbers are one run set from a third-party suite repo (kadyb/vector-benchmark, 23 stars, MIT) with no package versions; the Julia scripts there were added by GeometryOps contributors (commit history shows PR #12 and later Julia commits), so the suite is not fully independent of the library. The suite's detailed report page is on github.io and was not reachable; numbers come from timings.csv and the comparison.png in the repo (the two agree). GeometryOps' own README only points at this suite and says more benchmarks are coming. Julia is outside the 'usable from C++' scope.
found_via: Blogs / talks slice: opened JuliaGeo/GeometryOps.jl directly (Julia geometry ecosystem check) and followed its README 'Performance comparison to other packages' link to kadyb/vector-benchmark

name: Clipper (Clipper1 / polyclipping 6.4.2)
workload: Polygon clipping benchmark of several libraries (Boost.Geometry, Boost.Polygon, GEOS, SQL Server spatial types, TerraLib, Clipper) in a 2011 third-party blog post; per-test inputs unknown.
claimed_speedup: No numbers seen (search snippet only): 'Clipper is the fastest followed by Boost.Geometry, Sql Server ST and TerraLib'; in a longer test 'Boost.Geometry is the fastest' while 'Clipper starts better'; Boost.Geometry and GEOS give the best performance as the number of intersections increases.
stars_or_usage: 100,000+ lifetime SourceForge downloads; 4.8/5 on 37 reviews (SourceForge page)
tradeoffs: Vatti-style clipping and offsetting on integer coordinates; the SourceForge page says this library is obsolete and no longer maintained, superseded by Clipper2 (github.com/AngusJohnson/Clipper2, BSL-1.0, 2.5k stars, last commit 2026-04-20 as opened; its README makes no comparative performance claims and warns its triangulation code is buggy).
caveats: Snippet only: the blog page (rogue-modron.blogspot.com/2011/04/polygon-clipping-wrapper-benchmark.html, 'Polygon Clipping: a Wrapper, a Benchmark') returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, so no numbers, flags or hardware were seen, hence tier D. The benchmark is from 2011 and predates Clipper2 and current Boost.Geometry. The same snippet says Boost.Geometry wins when many intersections occur, so the win is workload dependent. The SourceForge page itself has no performance claims. No benchmark for Clipper2 against Boost.Geometry was found in this slice.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'polygon clipping library faster than Boost.Geometry benchmark blog' surfaced the 2011 rogue-modron.blogspot.com post (snippet only); opened the SourceForge project page for license and status

name: GeoDesk (libgeodesk)
baseline: SQL-based geospatial databases (README says 'SQL'; PostgreSQL/PostGIS is implied but not named)
workload: Feature queries (tag and spatial) on OpenStreetMap data in an in-process GOL file, plus GOL build time and storage size, versus a SQL-based database; no workload, dataset or hardware is described in the README.
claimed_speedup: Queries 'typically 50 times faster than SQL'; converting .osm.pbf to a GOL is '20 times faster than an import into an SQL database'; GOL files are 20% to 50% larger than the source PBF, 'less than a tenth of the storage consumed by a traditional SQL-based database'.
tradeoffs: Read-mostly embedded query engine on its own GOL file format for OpenStreetMap data, not a general geometry library; optional GEOS integration for buffer, union and similar operations; C++20; the GOL tool needs Java; query engine adds under 250 KB per the README.
caveats: First-party claim with no methodology, hardware, compiler or named baseline. The repo has benchmark/benchmark_main.cpp but its contents were not inspected. Narrow OSM-only domain, and the baseline is not one of Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS or R-tree baselines. Low confidence that it belongs in this category.
